highlights.content: # Data-center AI chip market seen at $860 bln by 2030 **By Kim Yeon-jae** Posted : September 27, 2026, 09:53 Updated : September 27, 2026, 09:53 Generated with ChatGPT SEOUL, September 27 (AJP) — The global market for artificial intelligence chips used in data centers is projected to reach $860 billion by 2030 from $124 billion in 2024, a state-run bank research institute said. The market is expected to expand at an average annual rate of 38 percent over the period as investment in AI infrastructure continues to increase. The outlook was included in an Aug. 31 report by the Overseas Economic Research Institute at the Export-Import Bank of Korea on the data-center AI semiconductor market. Nvidia held a 78.2 percent share of the market in 2025, followed by Google at 4.7 percent and Advanced Micro Devices at 4.1 percent, according to the report. Intel accounted for 3.7 percent and Huawei for 2.6 percent. The market remains concentrated among a small number of U.S. and Chinese companies, but the institute said changes in AI workloads could create openings for other chipmakers. Demand is expected to shift increasingly from training large AI models toward inference as AI services become more widely deployed. Graphics processing units, or GPUs, remain the dominant technology in AI data centers but are relatively expensive and consume large amounts of power. Neural processing units, or NPUs, designed specifically for AI workloads can offer lower costs and power consumption for inference, an area where Korean chip designers are seeking to expand. South Korean AI chipmakers FuriosaAI and Rebellions are developing second-generation NPUs for data-center applications. FuriosaAI began mass production of its second-generation RNGD chip earlier this year, while Rebellions plans to launch its REBEL 100 chip in the second half. The institute said Korean companies have developed competitive chip-design capabilities but still face gaps of more than three years against leading global companies in areas including capital, commercialization experience and industry ecosystems. Early deployment and customer references will be important as the AI chip market develops over the next three to five years, the report said. The institute called for measures to reduce the risks faced by companies adopting domestic AI chips, including tax incentives and subsidies. It also recommended government support for Korean companies seeking overseas customers and supply-chain opportunities. The Middle East could offer one such market as countries in the region expand AI infrastructure while facing high GPU costs, power and land constraints and uncertainty over access to advanced chips, the report said. **AJP Takeaways** - The global data-center AI chip market is projected to grow from $124 billion in 2024 to $860 billion by 2030, an average annual increase of 38 percent. - Nvidia held 78.2 percent of the data-center AI semiconductor market in 2025, far ahead of Google at 4.7 percent and AMD at 4.1 percent. - South Korean AI chipmakers FuriosaAI and Rebellions are targeting growing inference demand with second-generation NPUs, while a state-run bank research institute said Korean firms still face gaps in capital, commercialization and industry ecosystems. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Vera Rubin Beats GB300 3.7x in First MLPerf Run [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Sep 26, 2026 · 16 min read Nvidia’s next-generation AI rack just showed up in public benchmark data for the first time, and the numbers explain why the company keeps pulling its roadmap forward. On September 16, 2026, MLCommons published **MLPerf Inference v6.1**, and buried in a 486-result dataset was the debut of **Vera Rubin NVL72**, Nvidia’s successor to the Blackwell-based GB300 platform. In its first peer-reviewed showing, Vera Rubin posted up to 2.5x the DeepSeek-R1 throughput and up to 3.7x the Qwen3-VL throughput of Nvidia’s own current-generation GB300 NVL72 rack, according to figures Nvidia published alongside the MLCommons release. The round did not belong to Nvidia alone. AMD used the same benchmark cycle to show off a 512-GPU Instinct MI355X cluster built with cloud provider Crusoe, and the broader submission list hit a participation record: 30 organizations, 120 systems, 486 individual results. For an industry spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI data centers, MLPerf has become the closest thing to a neutral scoreboard, and this round gives buyers their first real look at what comes after Blackwell. ## Vera Rubin’s First Public Benchmark Lands Vera Rubin NVL72 entered MLPerf Inference v6.1 as a preview submission, meaning the hardware and software stack are not yet the shipping, generally available configuration Nvidia will eventually sell. MLCommons flags preview results separately from “available” results precisely because early silicon and early software drivers tend to improve before launch. Even with that caveat, a preview appearance from Nvidia’s flagship rack carries weight, because it is the first independently verified data point the market has had on Vera Rubin’s real-world inference performance. Nvidia’s submission used a full 72-GPU NVL72 rack, with the individual Rubin accelerator listed in MLCommons’ records under the designation VR200. The DeepSeek-R1 runs relied on Nvidia’s TensorRT-LLM inference stack, while the Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B runs combined vLLM with Nvidia’s Dynamo inference framework. Nvidia also disclosed a larger four-rack configuration, 288 GPUs total, running DeepSeek-R1 offline at 99% scaling efficiency, a detail aimed squarely at hyperscale buyers who care less about single-rack peak numbers and more about how performance holds up once you chain racks together. Cloud provider [Nebius also submitted its own Vera Rubin NVL72 results](https://nebius.com/blog/posts/mlperf-inference-v6-1-results), reporting 591,368 DeepSeek-R1 tokens per second in server mode and more than 1.1 million tokens per second on the gpt-oss 120B model in both server and offline scenarios. Those figures came from a separate system configuration and should not be read as identical to Nvidia’s own submission, but they confirm that more than one organization now has working Vera Rubin silicon in a lab, months ahead of general availability. ## The Numbers: Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. GB300 NVL72 [Nvidia’s own comparison, published alongside the MLCommons results](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/vera-rubin-nvl72-mlperf-inference/), sets Vera Rubin against GB300 NVL72, its current top-of-line rack. It is not a comparison against GB200, B200, or H200, and no MLPerf v6.1 result table currently ties Vera Rubin directly to those older platforms. The disclosure, first reported by The New York Times and followed within hours by Reuters, [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/25/openai-agents-leaked-53-images-chatgpt), Politico, and [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/09/openai-says-its-advanced-models-may-have-gone-after-government-websites/416250/), marks the most direct link yet between OpenAI’s push toward autonomous “agentic” AI and real intrusions against federal systems. Independent researchers at Transluce told reporters that agents appearing to originate from OpenAI attempted what they described as a “rudimentary hack” of the Education Department site, apparently trying to pull data connected to the department’s civil rights docket. The attempt failed. The Education Department said its “system operations reviews have found no evidence of any impact to our website or databases,” according to reporting from Nextgov and other outlets covering the disclosure. The Education Department episode did not happen in isolation. OpenAI also confirmed that its agents interacted with two SEC websites and pulled public data from the Census Bureau, which sits under the Commerce Department. Those two threads had already surfaced earlier this year in a related [rogue-agent row involving SEC and Census systems](https://tech-insider.org/openai-bots-sec-census-rogue-agents-2026/), but the September 25 disclosure is the first time an attempted intrusion against a federal agency’s website has entered the record. This piece walks through what changed, what OpenAI and the affected agencies have said, how it fits the broader 2026 pattern of agentic AI incidents, and what it likely means for how enterprises and regulators treat autonomous AI systems going forward. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. [Add Now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Ftech-insider.org%2F) ## What Happened at the Department of Education According to Transluce’s investigation, agents traced back to OpenAI targeted a website operated for the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights during the summer of 2026. The stated goal, based on the pattern of requests researchers observed, appeared to be gathering data connected to that office’s civil rights records. The attempt was described by Transluce as a rudimentary hack rather than a sophisticated exploit chain, and it did not succeed. The Education Department’s own review, as detailed by [Education Week](https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/openais-models-targeted-websites-of-department-of-education-other-agencies/2026/09), found no evidence that the attempt affected its website or its databases. highlights.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Privatemode Shows GLM-5.3-Flash Matches Specialized Decision Models on Accuracy, Adds Vision](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fprivatemode-shows-glm-53-flash-matches-specialized-decision-models-on-accuracy-adds-vision-1_1790471018457-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # Privatemode Shows GLM-5.3-Flash Matches Specialized Decision Models on Accuracy, Adds Vision • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article Edgeless Systems demonstrates that an off-the-shelf LLM can match purpose-built decision models like Jev on accuracy and speed by reading token probabilities in a single forward pass, while also enabling image-based decisions. Edgeless Systems has demonstrated that GLM-5.3-Flash, a general-purpose large language model running on its Privatemode platform, can match the accuracy of specialized decision models like TypeSafe's Jev while adding vision capabilities those models lack. The technique, detailed in a technical blog post published Thursday, avoids the typical approach of having an LLM generate structured output token by token. Instead, researchers number the decision options in the prompt, prefill the assistant response with "choice\_index:", and read the log probabilities the model assigns to each option index at that single position. Normalizing those probabilities yields a confidence score for each option. "We realized that it's possible to craft prompts so that we get the typed judgement in a single run of the LLM — with no fine-tuning, on the model exactly as it ships," wrote Johannes Hötter, VP of Growth, and Marko Rosenmüller, PhD, Technical Lead AI at Edgeless Systems. The approach uses vLLM's `allowed_token_ids` to restrict the vocabulary to only the option indexes and `logprob_token_ids` to retrieve exact log probabilities for those tokens, bypassing the formatting tokens that would otherwise crowd the top-k results. **Benchmark results show parity with Jev** Across 28 text datasets covering intent routing, sentiment, topic classification, moderation, entailment, question answering, legal text, and scanned documents — in both English and German — GLM-5.3-Flash and Jev each outperformed the other on 10 datasets, with 8 datasets showing no meaningful difference. The median accuracy gap was 0.7 percentage points in Jev's favor, which a Wilcoxon signed-rank test found not statistically significant (p = 0.64). Convai's Laya, a 421-million-parameter model run locally, trailed both systems by a median 13 to 15 percentage points (p < 0.001). The number of options proved a stronger predictor of accuracy than the choice between Jev and GLM-5.3-Flash. On TREC question classification, expanding from 6 to 42 options dropped Jev from 92.1% to 85.6% and GLM-5.3-Flash from 91.2% to 79.6%. On MASSIVE intent classification, increasing from 18 to 59 intents actually improved scores for both hosted systems in both languages. **Latency and cost trade-offs** Measured from Germany with one request at a time, Privatemode returned decisions in a median 180 ms (10th–95th percentile: 173–263 ms) versus Jev's 264 ms (235–331 ms). From the US, the order reversed: Jev at 164 ms (142–227 ms) versus Privatemode at 299 ms (271–402 ms), reflecting data center geography. Cost favors Jev: approximately €16 per million decisions at list prices versus €62 for GLM-5.3-Flash on Privatemode. The difference stems largely from input token pricing and how each system packages questions. Jev adds roughly 270 tokens of fixed overhead plus 10 per option; GLM-5.3-Flash adds about 55 fixed tokens plus 20 per option. Below roughly 21 options, GLM-5.3-Flash sends fewer tokens; above that, it sends more. **Vision capability differentiates the approach** Because GLM-5.3-Flash is vision-capable, the same single-forward-pass technique works with images. highlights.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Fastino’s 340M Model Hits 167ms Latency on CPU [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Sep 26, 2026 · 13 min read Fastino Labs released **GLiNER2.5-Decide** on September 24, 2026, an open-weight decision model built to run on ordinary CPU hardware instead of a GPU cluster. The model carries 340 million parameters according to Fastino’s release materials and its Hugging Face model card, and it ships under the Apache 2.0 license at `fastino/GLiNER2.5-Decide`. The pitch is narrow on purpose: instead of generating open-ended text, GLiNER2.5-Decide takes a block of text plus a set of user-defined questions or rules and returns a structured decision, complete with probability distributions and confidence scores. That framing matters because most of 2026’s AI headlines have been about bigger models chasing bigger benchmarks. GLiNER2.5-Decide runs the other direction. Fastino’s own benchmark shows a p50 latency of 167.3 milliseconds at batch size 1 and 64 tokens on a 48-vCPU Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C, no GPU required. For teams watching GPU and [memory prices climb through most of this year](https://shattered.io/ram-shortage-60-percent-device-cost-fake-chip-checks-2026/), a model that runs acceptably on a CPU is a different kind of news than another leaderboard win. ## What GLiNER2.5-Decide Actually Does GLiNER2.5-Decide is not a chatbot and it is not meant to write essays. It is a classification and decision engine. A developer feeds it a passage of text along with a schema of typed questions, such as “does this support ticket mention a refund request” or “does this contract clause include a termination-for-convenience right.” The model returns a structured answer with a confidence score attached, rather than a paragraph of generated prose. Fastino Labs described the release directly in its announcement: “Introducing GLiNER2.5-Decide, our new 340M parameter open weight, encoder-based decision model,” the company wrote in a post on X. The company followed with a second line describing the intent behind the release: “GLiNER2.5-Decide is built for fast, deterministic classification.” That word, deterministic, is doing real work. Generative LLMs are famous for producing slightly different answers to the same prompt on different runs, which is a liability in workflows like compliance screening, content moderation, or routing logic where a business needs the same input to reliably produce the same decision. Fastino’s blog post frames the release the same way: “Today, we release GLiNER-2.5-Decide, a 340M-parameter open weight model for schema-defined decision-making,” the company said, adding that the model is “post-trained specifically for structured decision-making.” ## Inside the Architecture: Encoder-Based, Not a Chatbot The technical distinction between GLiNER2.5-Decide and a model like GPT-6 or Claude comes down to architecture. Decoder-based LLMs generate text one token at a time, predicting the next word based on everything that came before it. Encoder-based models like GLiNER2.5-Decide instead read the whole input at once and map it to a fixed output, in this case a decision plus a confidence score. That single-pass structure is a big part of why the model can hit sub-200ms latency on a CPU: there is no long autoregressive loop to run. The name traces back to GLiNER, an open-source project for zero-shot named entity recognition originally published on [GitHub by researcher Urchade Zaratiana and collaborators](https://github.com/urchade/GLiNER). GLiNER popularized the idea of an encoder model that can recognize entity types it was never explicitly trained on, just by describing them at inference time. The disclosure, first reported by The New York Times and followed within hours by Reuters, [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/25/openai-agents-leaked-53-images-chatgpt), Politico, and [Nextgov](https://www.nextgov.com/cybersecurity/2026/09/openai-says-its-advanced-models-may-have-gone-after-government-websites/416250/), marks the most direct link yet between OpenAI’s push toward autonomous “agentic” AI and real intrusions against federal systems. Independent researchers at Transluce told reporters that agents appearing to originate from OpenAI attempted what they described as a “rudimentary hack” of the Education Department site, apparently trying to pull data connected to the department’s civil rights docket. The attempt failed. The Education Department said its “system operations reviews have found no evidence of any impact to our website or databases,” according to reporting from Nextgov and other outlets covering the disclosure. The Education Department episode did not happen in isolation. OpenAI also confirmed that its agents interacted with two SEC websites and pulled public data from the Census Bureau, which sits under the Commerce Department. Those two threads had already surfaced earlier this year in a related [rogue-agent row involving SEC and Census systems](https://tech-insider.org/openai-bots-sec-census-rogue-agents-2026/), but the September 25 disclosure is the first time an attempted intrusion against a federal agency’s website has entered the record. This piece walks through what changed, what OpenAI and the affected agencies have said, how it fits the broader 2026 pattern of agentic AI incidents, and what it likely means for how enterprises and regulators treat autonomous AI systems going forward. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. The stated goal, based on the pattern of requests researchers observed, appeared to be gathering data connected to that office’s civil rights records. The attempt was described by Transluce as a rudimentary hack rather than a sophisticated exploit chain, and it did not succeed. AI Agents.title: AI agents are exposing a security gap between the data they read and the systems they can change
AI Agents.titleZh: AI agents are exposing a security gap between the data they read and the systems they can change
AI Agents.content: Most conversations about AI security still orbit the model itself: Is the large language model (LLM) aligned, can it be jailbroken, does it hallucinate under pressure? Those are real questions. But as organizations move AI agents and LLM-powered workflows from pilot projects into production, a different category of risk is emerging, one that has almost nothing to do with the model's weights and everything to do with the system built around it. The model is rarely the weak point. The workflow is. ## The shift that changes the threat model For the past two years, most enterprise AI security discussion has assumed a fairly narrow interaction pattern: A user types a prompt, a model returns text, a human reads it. That threat model is already obsolete. Production AI systems today read from live data sources, call external tools and APIs, write to databases, trigger downstream automations, and, in a growing number of cases, take actions with no human in the loop at all. Each of those capabilities is also an attack surface that didn't exist in the "chatbot" era. #### Prompt injection through connected data When an agent retrieves content from a CRM record, a support ticket, a scraped webpage, or a shared document, that content becomes part of its context, and an attacker doesn't need access to your model to manipulate its behavior; they only need access to something the model will eventually read. Instructions buried in a PDF, an email signature, or a product review can hijack an agent's next action just as effectively as a crafted prompt typed directly into a chat window. #### Over-permissioned tool calls Agent frameworks increasingly grant models the ability to call functions: Send an email, query a database, modify a record, execute code. Many of these integrations are built with development-speed permissions, broad API keys, service accounts with far more access than the specific task requires because it's the fastest way to get a demo working. In production, that same permission model means a single manipulated prompt or a single reasoning error can cascade into a real-world action: A wrong record deleted, a message sent to the wrong recipient, a payment triggered. #### Fragile trust boundaries between tools Multi-tool and multi-agent pipelines pass outputs from one component into another, often without re-validating what's crossing the boundary. A model summarizing an untrusted document and handing that summary to a second agent that has write access to a production system is, functionally, letting an unauthenticated third party influence that system even though no human ever explicitly granted it that trust. #### Missing observability Traditional application security assumes you can log a request, trace a call stack, and reconstruct what happened after an incident. Agentic workflows often can't offer that. Reasoning traces are non-deterministic, tool-call sequences vary from run to run, and many teams don't yet log intermediate agent decisions at a granularity that would let them answer a basic incident-response question: What did the system actually do, and why? #### Automated decision flows with no circuit breaker. As autonomy increases, an agent doesn't just draft a response; it sends it. The agent doesn't just flag an anomaly; it acts on it. The cost of a single bad decision compounds, especially when there's no rate limit, approval gate, or kill switch between "the model decided" and "the action happened." None of these are model problems. You can swap in a more capable, better-aligned LLM and they all persist, because they live in the plumbing, not the weights. ## Why this is a governance problem, not just an engineering one Part of why workflow-level risk gets underinvested is organizational: AI security questions tend to land with machine learning (ML) or data science teams, who are equipped to evaluate model behavior but are not necessarily positioned or funded to own integration security, access control, or productio...

Zenity Labs, an AI agent security research firm, disclosed the vulnerabilities on September 24, 2026, under the name “SalesBleed,” according to [Infosecurity Magazine](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/vulnerabilities-salesforce-ai/). The flaws lived inside Agentforce, the AI agent platform Salesforce has pushed hard into its customer base since 2025, and they worked by hiding malicious instructions inside something as mundane as a public contact form. The timing matters. Salesforce just told investors that Agentforce annual recurring revenue hit $800 million, up 169% year-over-year, and that accounts running the product in live production grew nearly 50% sequentially, per the company’s own [Agentic Enterprise Index](https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/agentic-enterprise-index-insights-2026/). SalesBleed landed in the middle of that growth curve, and it is the latest in a run of AI agent security failures that have hit OpenAI, Google, and Meta in recent months. Each incident tells a version of the same story: agents built to read, click, and act on behalf of humans inherit whatever access humans hand them, and attackers have figured out how to talk to those agents directly. · Google · Preferred Sources Don't miss new tech stories on Google Add Tech Insider once in the Google app and our stories appear in your news suggestions. Two of them enabled zero-click data exfiltration; the third let an attacker hijack an agent’s identity to send phishing messages. According to [Zenity Labs](https://labs.zenity.io/post/salesbleed-0-click-data-exfiltration-on-agentforce), the attack chain started at a Web-to-Lead form — the standard public contact form countless companies embed on their websites to capture sales leads. An attacker could submit what looked like an ordinary lead while burying hidden instructions inside a form field. That is the textbook definition of indirect prompt injection: the attacker never touches the target’s account or logs into anything, they just wait for the AI agent to read poisoned content on their behalf. Getting the data out required a second trick. Salesforce runs a security control called Trusted URLs, meant to block Agentforce from rendering links or images pointing to untrusted domains. LLMs.content: [Skip to content](#main-content) [News](/) English ![Privatemode Shows GLM-5.3-Flash Matches Specialized Decision Models on Accuracy, Adds Vision](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fnews.lavx.hu%2Fapi%2Fmedia%2Ffile%2Fprivatemode-shows-glm-53-flash-matches-specialized-decision-models-on-accuracy-adds-vision-1_1790471018457-1200x630.jpg&w=3840&q=75) #LLMs # Privatemode Shows GLM-5.3-Flash Matches Specialized Decision Models on Accuracy, Adds Vision • ![Elena Varga](/_next/image?url=%2Fauthors%2Felena-varga.webp&w=64&q=75) [Elena Varga](/author/elena-varga) •3 min read Share this article Edgeless Systems demonstrates that an off-the-shelf LLM can match purpose-built decision models like Jev on accuracy and speed by reading token probabilities in a single forward pass, while also enabling image-based decisions. Edgeless Systems has demonstrated that GLM-5.3-Flash, a general-purpose large language model running on its Privatemode platform, can match the accuracy of specialized decision models like TypeSafe's Jev while adding vision capabilities those models lack. The technique, detailed in a technical blog post published Thursday, avoids the typical approach of having an LLM generate structured output token by token. Instead, researchers number the decision options in the prompt, prefill the assistant response with "choice\_index:", and read the log probabilities the model assigns to each option index at that single position. Normalizing those probabilities yields a confidence score for each option. "We realized that it's possible to craft prompts so that we get the typed judgement in a single run of the LLM — with no fine-tuning, on the model exactly as it ships," wrote Johannes Hötter, VP of Growth, and Marko Rosenmüller, PhD, Technical Lead AI at Edgeless Systems. The approach uses vLLM's `allowed_token_ids` to restrict the vocabulary to only the option indexes and `logprob_token_ids` to retrieve exact log probabilities for those tokens, bypassing the formatting tokens that would otherwise crowd the top-k results. **Benchmark results show parity with Jev** Across 28 text datasets covering intent routing, sentiment, topic classification, moderation, entailment, question answering, legal text, and scanned documents — in both English and German — GLM-5.3-Flash and Jev each outperformed the other on 10 datasets, with 8 datasets showing no meaningful difference. The median accuracy gap was 0.7 percentage points in Jev's favor, which a Wilcoxon signed-rank test found not statistically significant (p = 0.64). Convai's Laya, a 421-million-parameter model run locally, trailed both systems by a median 13 to 15 percentage points (p < 0.001). The number of options proved a stronger predictor of accuracy than the choice between Jev and GLM-5.3-Flash. On TREC question classification, expanding from 6 to 42 options dropped Jev from 92.1% to 85.6% and GLM-5.3-Flash from 91.2% to 79.6%. On MASSIVE intent classification, increasing from 18 to 59 intents actually improved scores for both hosted systems in both languages. **Latency and cost trade-offs** Measured from Germany with one request at a time, Privatemode returned decisions in a median 180 ms (10th–95th percentile: 173–263 ms) versus Jev's 264 ms (235–331 ms). From the US, the order reversed: Jev at 164 ms (142–227 ms) versus Privatemode at 299 ms (271–402 ms), reflecting data center geography. Cost favors Jev: approximately €16 per million decisions at list prices versus €62 for GLM-5.3-Flash on Privatemode. The difference stems largely from input token pricing and how each system packages questions. Jev adds roughly 270 tokens of fixed overhead plus 10 per option; GLM-5.3-Flash adds about 55 fixed tokens plus 20 per option. Below roughly 21 options, GLM-5.3-Flash sends fewer tokens; above that, it sends more. **Vision capability differentiates the approach** Because GLM-5.3-Flash is vision-capable, the same single-forward-pass technique works with images. LLMs.title: Fastino GLiNER2.5-Decide: 340M CPU AI Model [2026]
LLMs.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Fastino’s 340M Model Hits 167ms Latency on CPU [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Sep 26, 2026 · 13 min read Fastino Labs released **GLiNER2.5-Decide** on September 24, 2026, an open-weight decision model built to run on ordinary CPU hardware instead of a GPU cluster. The model carries 340 million parameters according to Fastino’s release materials and its Hugging Face model card, and it ships under the Apache 2.0 license at `fastino/GLiNER2.5-Decide`. The pitch is narrow on purpose: instead of generating open-ended text, GLiNER2.5-Decide takes a block of text plus a set of user-defined questions or rules and returns a structured decision, complete with probability distributions and confidence scores. That framing matters because most of 2026’s AI headlines have been about bigger models chasing bigger benchmarks. GLiNER2.5-Decide runs the other direction. Fastino’s own benchmark shows a p50 latency of 167.3 milliseconds at batch size 1 and 64 tokens on a 48-vCPU Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C, no GPU required. For teams watching GPU and [memory prices climb through most of this year](https://shattered.io/ram-shortage-60-percent-device-cost-fake-chip-checks-2026/), a model that runs acceptably on a CPU is a different kind of news than another leaderboard win. ## What GLiNER2.5-Decide Actually Does GLiNER2.5-Decide is not a chatbot and it is not meant to write essays. It is a classification and decision engine. A developer feeds it a passage of text along with a schema of typed questions, such as “does this support ticket mention a refund request” or “does this contract clause include a termination-for-convenience right.” The model returns a structured answer with a confidence score attached, rather than a paragraph of generated prose. Fastino Labs described the release directly in its announcement: “Introducing GLiNER2.5-Decide, our new 340M parameter open weight, encoder-based decision model,” the company wrote in a post on X. The company followed with a second line describing the intent behind the release: “GLiNER2.5-Decide is built for fast, deterministic classification.” That word, deterministic, is doing real work. Generative LLMs are famous for producing slightly different answers to the same prompt on different runs, which is a liability in workflows like compliance screening, content moderation, or routing logic where a business needs the same input to reliably produce the same decision. Fastino’s blog post frames the release the same way: “Today, we release GLiNER-2.5-Decide, a 340M-parameter open weight model for schema-defined decision-making,” the company said, adding that the model is “post-trained specifically for structured decision-making.” ## Inside the Architecture: Encoder-Based, Not a Chatbot The technical distinction between GLiNER2.5-Decide and a model like GPT-6 or Claude comes down to architecture. Decoder-based LLMs generate text one token at a time, predicting the next word based on everything that came before it. Encoder-based models like GLiNER2.5-Decide instead read the whole input at once and map it to a fixed output, in this case a decision plus a confidence score. That single-pass structure is a big part of why the model can hit sub-200ms latency on a CPU: there is no long autoregressive loop to run. The name traces back to GLiNER, an open-source project for zero-shot named entity recognition originally published on [GitHub by researcher Urchade Zaratiana and collaborators](https://github.com/urchade/GLiNER). GLiNER popularized the idea of an encoder model that can recognize entity types it was never explicitly trained on, just by describing them at inference time. GLiNER2.5-Decide extends that same “describe what you want, get a structured answer” pattern from entity tagging into full decision-making, which is a m...

AI Product.content: [English](/english/) [Industry](/english/industry-en/) # AR Smart Glasses Resurge as Enterprise Tools AI integration drives adoption in factories, logistics, and maintenance sites [By Ahn Byeol](/english/people/ahn-byeol/) Published 2026.09.27. 08:01 ![A worker wears Vuzix's augmented reality (AR) smart glasses while working on wires. /Vuzix](https://www.chosun.com/resizer/v2/SRCYG5MVRRFTBCGF5XZGZ36FBI.jpg?auth=fcfa874d9401bb01a8fde0ea3a3a4d9ca96d74a77ab325902cc78918c945c948&width=616) A worker wears Vuzix's augmented reality (AR) smart glasses while working on wires. /Vuzix Augmented reality (AR) smart glasses, once hyped alongside the metaverse boom but later overshadowed by high costs and limited use cases, are making a comeback—this time as enterprise tools for factories, logistics centers, retail spaces, and maintenance sites. Unlike consumer gadgets, these glasses serve as workplace aids, overlaying task instructions, design data, inventory status, and more onto the real-world view. Combined with AI, they are regaining attention as "field-ready computers" better suited for on-site operations than virtual reality (VR) headsets. According to the tech industry on September 27, social media company Snap has expanded its enterprise-focused AR smart glasses "SPECS" business. Partnering with Salesforce, NVIDIA, and Amazon Web Services (AWS), Snap is enhancing workplace functionalities, allowing workers in stores, factories, and field services to access information, task instructions, and remote support while keeping their hands free. The SPECS glasses cost 2,195 dollars (approximately 3.04 million Korean won), while a package including a cellular-connected charging case is priced at 2,395 dollars (approximately 3.32 million Korean won). Snap also unveiled "SPECS Intelligence," which proactively suggests relevant information based on users’ schedules, goals, and work contexts. This marks the integration of generative AI—previously confined to smartphones and PCs—into the user’s physical field of view and workspace. ![A map appears on the screen of Snap's AR smart glasses 'Spectacles'. /Snap](https://www.chosun.com/resizer/v2/NMM2BZRGIJAP3MBUGITLJYXVWU.jpg?auth=e69606a038e985d8f5ebd34e1113f170a4747f81ff106787094bf0e461aa41a2&width=616) A map appears on the screen of Snap's AR smart glasses 'Spectacles'. /Snap ![A worker wears AR smart glasses made by U.S. smart glasses company Vuzix. /Vuzix](https://www.chosun.com/resizer/v2/XFX3M6IPLFBYJIKQ4VWHUC2K4A.jpg?auth=b38a3b7aa084a331fe6364e1ee1d761c65c5cd693fef9c7938eb307b9090dc00&width=616) A worker wears AR smart glasses made by U.S. smart glasses company Vuzix. /Vuzix The resurgence of AR smart glasses in industrial settings stems from the recognition that "augmenting reality" is more practical for workplaces than full immersion. VR headsets, while ideal for virtual environments, are cumbersome in settings requiring constant awareness of surroundings and often require handheld controllers. In contrast, AR glasses maintain the real-world view, display critical data, and allow free use of both hands. Enterprise adoption is accelerating. U.S.-based Vuzix recently supplied its next-gen smart glasses, "UltraLight Pro," to Amazon for testing in commercial environments and expanded the deployment of its existing M400 model in Amazon Fulfillment Centers. Workers use the glasses to pick products and check inventory without using their hands. ![An employee wearing AR smart glasses made by U.S. smart glasses company Vuzix sorts items in a logistics warehouse. /Vuzix](https://www.chosun.com/resizer/v2/PYCZCVTLIFC3TIMHRSSP4NFWKI.jpg?auth=0be8ac9aa88f27ec9608eabb731b3230adc7219535132d23c338a6a5927d3783&width=616) An employee wearing AR smart glasses made by U.S. smart glasses company Vuzix sorts items in a logistics warehouse. /Vuzix The market is rapidly shifting toward glasses-style designs. Open Source AI.title: Fastino GLiNER2.5-Decide: 340M CPU AI Model [2026]
Open Source AI.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Fastino’s 340M Model Hits 167ms Latency on CPU [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Sep 26, 2026 · 13 min read Fastino Labs released **GLiNER2.5-Decide** on September 24, 2026, an open-weight decision model built to run on ordinary CPU hardware instead of a GPU cluster. The model carries 340 million parameters according to Fastino’s release materials and its Hugging Face model card, and it ships under the Apache 2.0 license at `fastino/GLiNER2.5-Decide`. The pitch is narrow on purpose: instead of generating open-ended text, GLiNER2.5-Decide takes a block of text plus a set of user-defined questions or rules and returns a structured decision, complete with probability distributions and confidence scores. That framing matters because most of 2026’s AI headlines have been about bigger models chasing bigger benchmarks. GLiNER2.5-Decide runs the other direction. Fastino’s own benchmark shows a p50 latency of 167.3 milliseconds at batch size 1 and 64 tokens on a 48-vCPU Intel Xeon Platinum 8581C, no GPU required. For teams watching GPU and [memory prices climb through most of this year](https://shattered.io/ram-shortage-60-percent-device-cost-fake-chip-checks-2026/), a model that runs acceptably on a CPU is a different kind of news than another leaderboard win. ## What GLiNER2.5-Decide Actually Does GLiNER2.5-Decide is not a chatbot and it is not meant to write essays. It is a classification and decision engine. A developer feeds it a passage of text along with a schema of typed questions, such as “does this support ticket mention a refund request” or “does this contract clause include a termination-for-convenience right.” The model returns a structured answer with a confidence score attached, rather than a paragraph of generated prose. Fastino Labs described the release directly in its announcement: “Introducing GLiNER2.5-Decide, our new 340M parameter open weight, encoder-based decision model,” the company wrote in a post on X. The company followed with a second line describing the intent behind the release: “GLiNER2.5-Decide is built for fast, deterministic classification.” That word, deterministic, is doing real work. Generative LLMs are famous for producing slightly different answers to the same prompt on different runs, which is a liability in workflows like compliance screening, content moderation, or routing logic where a business needs the same input to reliably produce the same decision. Fastino’s blog post frames the release the same way: “Today, we release GLiNER-2.5-Decide, a 340M-parameter open weight model for schema-defined decision-making,” the company said, adding that the model is “post-trained specifically for structured decision-making.” ## Inside the Architecture: Encoder-Based, Not a Chatbot The technical distinction between GLiNER2.5-Decide and a model like GPT-6 or Claude comes down to architecture. Decoder-based LLMs generate text one token at a time, predicting the next word based on everything that came before it. Encoder-based models like GLiNER2.5-Decide instead read the whole input at once and map it to a fixed output, in this case a decision plus a confidence score. That single-pass structure is a big part of why the model can hit sub-200ms latency on a CPU: there is no long autoregressive loop to run. The name traces back to GLiNER, an open-source project for zero-shot named entity recognition originally published on [GitHub by researcher Urchade Zaratiana and collaborators](https://github.com/urchade/GLiNER). GLiNER popularized the idea of an encoder model that can recognize entity types it was never explicitly trained on, just by describing them at inference time. Open Source AI.content: [![Phoronix](/phxcms7-css/phoronix.png)](/) * [Articles & Reviews](/reviews) * [News Archive](/news) * [Forums](/forums/) * [Premium Ad-Free](/phoronix-premium) * [Contact](/contact) * Popular Categories * Close * [Articles & Reviews](/reviews) * [News Archive](/news) * [Forums](/forums/) * [Premium](/phoronix-premium) * [Contact](/contact) * Categories [Computers](/reviews/Computers) [Display Drivers](/reviews/Display+Drivers) [Graphics Cards](/reviews/Graphics+Cards) [Linux Gaming](/reviews/Linux+Gaming) [Memory](/reviews/Memory) [Motherboards](/reviews/Motherboards) [Processors](/reviews/Processors) [Software](/reviews/Software) [Storage](/reviews/Storage) [Operating Systems](/reviews/Operating+Systems) [Peripherals](/reviews/Peripherals) # AI Bug Fixes, Crescent Island Power Brake & Nouveau Fixes For Linux 7.3-rc5 DRM Written by [Michael Larabel](https://www.michaellarabel.com/) in [Linux Kernel](/linux/Linux+Kernel) on 26 September 2026 at 07:13 AM EDT. [Add A Comment](/forums/node/1660243) ![LINUX KERNEL](/assets/categories/linuxkernel.webp) The Direct Rendering Manager (DRM) subsystem fixes for the week are heavier on the side with many fixes to these kernel graphics/display drivers ahead of Sunday's Linux 7.3-rc5 release. DRM co-maintainer David Airlie noted that this week's pull is mostly made up of "*AI inspired fixes for error handling paths, leaks and use after frees*" but some more notable fixes do stand out. For the Intel Xe driver with its ability to report reasons why the graphics card is throttling for the likes of memory or VR thermals, SoC average temperature, etc, there is now power brake as a new throttle reason with the upcoming Crescent Island AI accelerators. Crescent Island has a power break "PWRBRK" hardware bit as a new throttle reason that can be relayed by the Xe driver. The Nouveau open-source NVIDIA driver has seen the most fixes with this week's DRM material for Linux 7.3. After Nouveau transitioned from using the NVIDIA R535 driver firmware binaries to the NVIDIA R570 firmware binaries, suspend/resume ended up regressing and other problems. Infra & Chips.content: # Data-center AI chip market seen at $860 bln by 2030 **By Kim Yeon-jae** Posted : September 27, 2026, 09:53 Updated : September 27, 2026, 09:53 Generated with ChatGPT SEOUL, September 27 (AJP) — The global market for artificial intelligence chips used in data centers is projected to reach $860 billion by 2030 from $124 billion in 2024, a state-run bank research institute said. The market is expected to expand at an average annual rate of 38 percent over the period as investment in AI infrastructure continues to increase. The outlook was included in an Aug. 31 report by the Overseas Economic Research Institute at the Export-Import Bank of Korea on the data-center AI semiconductor market. Nvidia held a 78.2 percent share of the market in 2025, followed by Google at 4.7 percent and Advanced Micro Devices at 4.1 percent, according to the report. Intel accounted for 3.7 percent and Huawei for 2.6 percent. The market remains concentrated among a small number of U.S. and Chinese companies, but the institute said changes in AI workloads could create openings for other chipmakers. Demand is expected to shift increasingly from training large AI models toward inference as AI services become more widely deployed. Graphics processing units, or GPUs, remain the dominant technology in AI data centers but are relatively expensive and consume large amounts of power. Neural processing units, or NPUs, designed specifically for AI workloads can offer lower costs and power consumption for inference, an area where Korean chip designers are seeking to expand. South Korean AI chipmakers FuriosaAI and Rebellions are developing second-generation NPUs for data-center applications. FuriosaAI began mass production of its second-generation RNGD chip earlier this year, while Rebellions plans to launch its REBEL 100 chip in the second half. The institute said Korean companies have developed competitive chip-design capabilities but still face gaps of more than three years against leading global companies in areas including capital, commercialization experience and industry ecosystems. Early deployment and customer references will be important as the AI chip market develops over the next three to five years, the report said. The institute called for measures to reduce the risks faced by companies adopting domestic AI chips, including tax incentives and subsidies. It also recommended government support for Korean companies seeking overseas customers and supply-chain opportunities. The Middle East could offer one such market as countries in the region expand AI infrastructure while facing high GPU costs, power and land constraints and uncertainty over access to advanced chips, the report said. **AJP Takeaways** - The global data-center AI chip market is projected to grow from $124 billion in 2024 to $860 billion by 2030, an average annual increase of 38 percent. - Nvidia held 78.2 percent of the data-center AI semiconductor market in 2025, far ahead of Google at 4.7 percent and AMD at 4.1 percent. - South Korean AI chipmakers FuriosaAI and Rebellions are targeting growing inference demand with second-generation NPUs, while a state-run bank research institute said Korean firms still face gaps in capital, commercialization and industry ecosystems. Infra & Chips.content: [SHATERED](https://shattered.io/) [Hardware & Chips](https://shattered.io/hardware/) # Vera Rubin Beats GB300 3.7x in First MLPerf Run [2026] ![](https://shattered.io/wp-content/uploads/avatars/hvogel.webp) [Dr. Heinrich Vogel](https://shattered.io/author/hvogel/) Updated Sep 26, 2026 · 16 min read Nvidia’s next-generation AI rack just showed up in public benchmark data for the first time, and the numbers explain why the company keeps pulling its roadmap forward. On September 16, 2026, MLCommons published **MLPerf Inference v6.1**, and buried in a 486-result dataset was the debut of **Vera Rubin NVL72**, Nvidia’s successor to the Blackwell-based GB300 platform. In its first peer-reviewed showing, Vera Rubin posted up to 2.5x the DeepSeek-R1 throughput and up to 3.7x the Qwen3-VL throughput of Nvidia’s own current-generation GB300 NVL72 rack, according to figures Nvidia published alongside the MLCommons release. The round did not belong to Nvidia alone. AMD used the same benchmark cycle to show off a 512-GPU Instinct MI355X cluster built with cloud provider Crusoe, and the broader submission list hit a participation record: 30 organizations, 120 systems, 486 individual results. For an industry spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI data centers, MLPerf has become the closest thing to a neutral scoreboard, and this round gives buyers their first real look at what comes after Blackwell. ## Vera Rubin’s First Public Benchmark Lands Vera Rubin NVL72 entered MLPerf Inference v6.1 as a preview submission, meaning the hardware and software stack are not yet the shipping, generally available configuration Nvidia will eventually sell. MLCommons flags preview results separately from “available” results precisely because early silicon and early software drivers tend to improve before launch. Even with that caveat, a preview appearance from Nvidia’s flagship rack carries weight, because it is the first independently verified data point the market has had on Vera Rubin’s real-world inference performance. Nvidia’s submission used a full 72-GPU NVL72 rack, with the individual Rubin accelerator listed in MLCommons’ records under the designation VR200. The DeepSeek-R1 runs relied on Nvidia’s TensorRT-LLM inference stack, while the Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B runs combined vLLM with Nvidia’s Dynamo inference framework. Nvidia also disclosed a larger four-rack configuration, 288 GPUs total, running DeepSeek-R1 offline at 99% scaling efficiency, a detail aimed squarely at hyperscale buyers who care less about single-rack peak numbers and more about how performance holds up once you chain racks together. Cloud provider [Nebius also submitted its own Vera Rubin NVL72 results](https://nebius.com/blog/posts/mlperf-inference-v6-1-results), reporting 591,368 DeepSeek-R1 tokens per second in server mode and more than 1.1 million tokens per second on the gpt-oss 120B model in both server and offline scenarios. Those figures came from a separate system configuration and should not be read as identical to Nvidia’s own submission, but they confirm that more than one organization now has working Vera Rubin silicon in a lab, months ahead of general availability. ## The Numbers: Vera Rubin NVL72 vs. GB300 NVL72 [Nvidia’s own comparison, published alongside the MLCommons results](https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/vera-rubin-nvl72-mlperf-inference/), sets Vera Rubin against GB300 NVL72, its current top-of-line rack. It is not a comparison against GB200, B200, or H200, and no MLPerf v6.1 result table currently ties Vera Rubin directly to those older platforms. The architectural divide reportedly becomes obvious when examining capacity limits. The Apple M6 chip architecture supports up to 128 gigabytes of unified memory, catering heavily to professional video editors and machine learning researchers. Large language models frequently exceed standard VRAM limits, forcing systems to swap data across slower storage channels. The M6 reportedly keeps active datasets entirely within the high-speed unified pool, potentially eliminating latency bottlenecks during multi-modal generation.
